journal_name: ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems

abstracts.abstract: The design of large-scale autonomous systems increasingly requires coordination mechanisms that can handle emergent behaviors and dynamic environments. Traditional control-theoretic approaches often struggle to capture the inherent complexity and heterogeneity of modern distributed systems. This paper introduces a novel theoretical paradigm grounded in Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) theory to fundamentally reimagine the design of decentralized autonomous systems. We formalize a meta-control framework that models system dynamics through local interaction rules and their resulting global emergence patterns. The framework establishes rigorous mappings between microscopic behavioral rules and macroscopic system properties, enabling formal verification of self-organizing behaviors. Key contributions include: (1) a formal specification language for describing adaptive coordination in multi-agent settings; (2) proof of necessary and sufficient conditions for emergent coordination under varying network topologies; and (3) theoretical bounds on system resilience under component failures. Unlike existing approaches that treat emergence as an artifact to be managed, our paradigm embraces emergent phenomena as a design primitive. We demonstrate the framework's applicability through analysis of representative autonomous system scenarios, showing how decentralized control can achieve global objectives without centralized coordination. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for designing autonomous systems where adaptability, scalability, and robustness arise naturally from local interactions.

Runtime decision-making in self-adaptive software systems requires effective handling of environmental uncertainty and dynamic requirement changes. While Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) provide a solid foundation for modeling such sequential decision problems, conventional solution approaches suffer from significant limitations when confronted with the high variability characteristic of real-world deployment contexts. This paper presents a Robust MDP framework that substantially advances the state of the art in adaptive decision-making under uncertainty. Our approach introduces distributional uncertainty sets that capture both parameter variation and environmental volatility, enabling the derivation of policies that perform reliably across a range of plausible system states. We develop novel solution techniques based on robust optimization principles and approximate dynamic programming that maintain decision-making tractability while providing strong performance guarantees. The theoretical analysis establishes three key results: (1) finite-sample bounds on policy performance degradation under uncertainty; (2) structural properties of optimal robust policies that enable efficient computation; and (3) conditions under which robust solutions exhibit superior generalization to novel environments. Empirical evaluation across multiple adaptive system domains demonstrates that our framework achieves 35-45% improvement in worst-case performance compared to standard expected-value approaches while maintaining comparable average-case behavior. This work provides both theoretical foundations and practical algorithms for building self-adaptive systems with principled robustness guarantees.

Current adaptive systems typically employ hierarchical feedback control loops that treat adaptation as a reactive correction mechanism. However, this paradigm proves inadequate for autonomous systems operating in complex, multi-dimensional environments where multiple adaptation objectives must be balanced simultaneously. We introduce CogniAdapt, a fundamentally different architecture that endows autonomous systems with cognitive capabilities for proactive, context-aware adaptation. The architecture implements a computational consciousness model that maintains awareness of system state, environmental conditions, and ongoing adaptation processes. At its core, CogniAdapt integrates perception, deliberation, and action components through a unified cognitive cycle that enables principled reasoning about adaptation trade-offs. The system employs a hierarchical planning mechanism that distinguishes between tactical adaptations (responding to immediate stimuli) and strategic adaptations (optimizing long-term system properties). We provide a complete reference implementation that demonstrates the architecture's effectiveness in managing cloud resource allocation under variable workloads and security threats. Experimental results reveal that CogniAdapt achieves 52% better performance on composite utility metrics compared to state-of-the-art MAPE-K approaches, while exhibiting more stable adaptation behavior with reduced oscillation. The architecture naturally supports explainability through its cognitive state representation, enabling stakeholders to understand and verify adaptation decisions. This work establishes a new design paradigm for autonomous systems where intelligent adaptation emerges from cognitive principles rather than engineered rules.

Multi-agent systems increasingly require sophisticated coordination capabilities to operate effectively in adversarial or congested environments. While deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising approach for training cooperative behaviors, existing methods exhibit critical limitations including sample inefficiency, training instability, and poor generalization to novel scenarios. This paper presents AdaptCoord, a substantially improved multi-agent coordination framework that addresses these fundamental challenges. AdaptCoord introduces three key innovations: (1) a graph-structured communication topology learned dynamically based on task requirements, replacing static all-to-all communication; (2) an attention-based value decomposition scheme that enables graceful handling of variable team sizes and compositions; and (3) a curriculum-driven training procedure that progressively introduces environmental complexity to accelerate learning. The system architecture employs centralized training with decentralized execution, maintaining coordination capability while preserving individual agent autonomy. We provide a full implementation integrated with the Ray/RLlib ecosystem, enabling seamless deployment in realistic autonomous system applications. Extensive evaluation across cooperative navigation, cooperative pushing, and mixed adversarial domains demonstrates that AdaptCoord achieves 67% higher sample efficiency compared to baseline methods while exhibiting superior zero-shot transfer to unseen scenarios. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of each architectural component. The framework has been validated in a simulated swarm robotics application involving 50+ agents, demonstrating practical scalability. This work delivers a production-ready solution for multi-agent coordination that substantially advances the state of practice.
